My first choice is "American Lion", by Jon Meacham. I'm working through it now. It's a terrific biography of Andrew Jackson.

As Meacham describes the climate within which Jackson took office, I find myself seeing parallels between the social trends of the 1820s and today. I encountered the following paragraph just now, and it inspired me to make this post:

Recording some "small gossiping anecdotes" in his diary, John Quincy Adams reported how "indignant" a Jackson caller had been when introduced to the president-elect "as an Aristocrat." Democracy was in; elitism was out. New forces were being unleashed and new paths taken "When he comes, he will bring a breeze with him," [Daniel] Webster said of Jackson. "Which way it will blow, I cannot tell." He was not the only one.

Jackson gave his opponents plenty of ammo to use against him. One of their favorite sticking points was his famed temper. And he certainly had one, routinely challenging slanderers to duels (especially when they were stupid enough to defame his dearest Emily). It was said that a man of such overt passion had no business in the land's highest office. But despite his known temper, Jackson was a man of tremendous charisma, congeniality and social grace. He glided between fits of passion and eloquent discourse, and, to the outside observer, it was seamless. He was a consummate socialite, taking command of any ball or gala or party where he found himself. All this was a means to be the great man his late mother wished him to be.

Jackson's election into office was a bit of an upset. Henry Clay (SecState) believed he was a shoe in for the office. Jackson believe that, in the previous election (when he lost), Clay had sold his votes to John Quincy Adams in exchange for the cabinet appointment, a position from which presidents tended to spring. He believed it without question, and no one would ever convince him otherwise. In fact, when the results were beginning to favor Jackson, Clay would go on to say that the fact the election was even close was "mortifying and sickening to the hearts of the real lovers of free Government." And when Jackson's victory was assured, "no greater calamity" had struck the United States "since we were a free people." [p. 49]

Clay was a dyed-in-the-wool Federalist - a party that believed strongly in, among other things, limited suffrage and limiting sovereignty to the few. They were the adherents of one Alexander Hamilton, while their opponents, the Democratic-Republicans, were followers of an entirely Jeffersonian philosophy. Jackson was elected when almost all states had legislated suffrage to all white European males. He won 56% of the popular vote, which gave him the electoral votes he needed: the electoral count was 178-83.

This was an era when race, religion, and the role of women was in the forefront of the national dialogue, for what it was in a time of limited communication, although that, too, was evolving, as steamships began making regular trans-Atlantic trips, and railways began to connect the nation. Atheism was beginning to receive a national platform, and thrust itself headlong into ideological opposition with the prevailing Christian ideologies of the new nation. Jackson himself was a firm believer in the grace of divine Providence, and unwaveringly placed his faith in his Creator. He even went as far to say that Christian values were the most influential and reflective of the nation's values.
